qa_warnings: caution: treatment wording (fine in a caveat; the reviewer judges claims): 'treat insomnia'
blocking: Two dead links: both www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10604906/ and PMC11059092/ return 404. Neither pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov version is on the allowed list, so neither link can be repointed. The 90.6% figure is also wrong: the paper's own Results and Table 1 give 93.5%. The fix is to remove both specific claims and keep the section's point by drawing on an allowed source the article already cites. The Spain and Turkish-teen statistics also didn't fit the reader, since the 'problematic smartphone use' framing sits close to addiction language.

The systematic review claim goes further than the source (fact-check claim 6). Only five of the seven self-report studies ran 28 to 30 days. The three studies with objective measures used one-day protocols, and readers need that to understand why objective results were inconclusive.

The Tapert quote is shown as a complete sentence, but the original sentence continues ('...and we process it more intensely'). The fix adds an ellipsis to mark it as partial. Her title also needs correcting: the source describes her as a psychiatry professor.

The Exelmans sample were young adults (a convenience sample aged 18 to 25), not 'adults'. The fact-check also found the 39-minute gap was linked to media use around the evening, not specifically to media use in bed. Wording changed to 'young adults' and 'evening media use'. Per the brief, the age range is not given.

Fact-check claim 6 is still open. The abstract does not say three studies measured sleep objectively: it lists actigraphy (n = 2) and polysomnography (n = 3), which may overlap. Cut the count so the sentence matches the source.

This overstates the Exelmans source (fact-check claim 3). That study links the 39-minute shuteye latency to pre-bedtime media use and says nothing about revenge bedtime procrastination. Frame the link as our own reading.
The '30 to 60 minutes' advice has no source (the fact-check marked it UNSUPPORTED). Our rules require a source for specific numeric claims, so reword it as no evidence-based cutoff.
